newsitem.title: USA: Shipwrecks found along Mediterranean trade route.
newsitem.headline: Shipwrecks found along Mediterranean trade route.

text.p: A newly discovered cluster of eight shipwrecks in deep water along an ancient trade route suggests the Mediterranean Sea may harbour its own Bermuda Triangle, an archaeologist said on Wednesday.

Five of the vessels date from between 100 B.C. and 400 A.D., while the other three range in age from 100 to more than 200 years. All are located about 2,500 feet (760 metres) underwater at a 20 square mile (51.80 sq km) site about equidistant from Tunisia, Sicily and Sardinia.

The wrecks were found with the help of a wheeled U.S. Navy research submarine that literally rolled along the bottom of the Mediterranean, using long-range sonar to locate the ships. A remote-controlled robot vessel was then used to collect 115 artifacts, archaeologist Robert Ballard said in a telephone interview.

Because so many wrecks were found in such deep water so close together, Ballard and others on his team suggested that this may be an area of sudden, violent storms where ships sink quickly without a trace on the surface, analogous to the so-called Bermuda Triangle,the vast three-sided segment of the Atlantic Ocean bordered by Bermuda, Puerto Rico and Fort Lauderdale, Florida.

Most previously discovered shipwrecks have been found in water less than 200 feet (61 metres), close enough to shore to permit looting and damage from surf, and earlier explorers surmised that ancient mariners sailed close to the coastline.

But Ballard said these finds, made in May and June, indicate ancient sailors braved deep waters and rough seas as they followed a trade route between what is now western Italy near Rome and what is now the city of Tunis.

The advantage to such deep wrecks, Ballard said, is that the cold water and inaccessibility helps to preserve the ships and their cargo. Wood-eating organisms destroy any part of the ships that lies above the bottom mud, but other materials are in a kind of natural cold-storage.

The artifacts from the eight wrecks include kitchen and household wares, bronze vessels, two heavy lead anchor stocks, eight long-necked jars called amphora intended for wine, olive oil, fish sauce and preserved fruit, archaeologist Anna Marguerite McCann said in a statement released by the National Geographic Society, which helped fund the expedition.
"Sampling the splendidly preserved cargo of cooking wares in this wreck is like shopping in a Roman kitchenware outlet," another archaeologist, John Oleson, said in the statement.

One vessel that may date from the first century A.D. carried a heavy cargo of marble or granite building stones, including some monolithic columns that suggest materials for a temple or other structure, Ballard said.
Ballard said there are no plans to raise any of the wrecks because they and their cargoes are secure where they lie.
Ballard is president of the Institute for Exploration, based in Mystic, Connecticut, which is dedicated to deep-sea archaeology. He said his next expedition will be to the Black Sea.
